title: Superstore
synopsis: It's 9:43 p.m. at Cloud 9. The corporate inspector is hiding in Aisle 7, a man has fallen asleep in a kayak, and somebody — possibly Jonah — set off the indoor sprinklers in Pets. You have seventeen minutes to close. Good luck.

nodes.text: Glenn announces over the PA that the store will close in seventeen minutes. He then thanks the customers for their patience by name, which slows everyone down. Amy gives you the closer's look — equal parts faith and warning. reports normal conditions.

choices.text: Start the closing checklist top-down
choices.consequence: Order is a kind of prayer. You start the closing checklist top-down. The path to The Checklist opens, and the system registers the move before anyone admits the rules have changed.

choices.text: Just start chasing customers out, gently
choices.consequence: Aim at the exits, not the aisles. You commit to just start chasing customers out, gently. It carries you toward The Stragglers, exchanging a familiar uncertainty for a consequence nobody has modeled.

nodes.text: You grab the laminated checklist. Step one: cash counts. Step two: zone the front. Step three: locate Marcus, who is somewhere in the store, possibly asleep in outdoor furnishings. “Cash count first, by the book” draws you toward Cash Drawer Trouble; “Locate Marcus first, by the smell” leaves Marcus Found waiting on the other side.

choices.text: Cash count first, by the book
choices.consequence: Cash trouble is the worst trouble. You commit to cash count first, by the book. It carries you toward Cash Drawer Trouble, exchanging a familiar uncertainty for a consequence nobody has modeled.

choices.text: Locate Marcus first, by the smell
choices.consequence: Lose a coworker, lose your night. You choose to locate Marcus first, by the smell. By Marcus Found, the decision has become data, precedent, and a problem larger than the person who made it.

nodes.text: There's a man in the kayak, two teenagers using the patio set as a movie theater, and a woman who has been comparing two identical jars of pickles for forty-one minutes. You have, at most, three minutes of polite-voice.

choices.text: Use polite-voice on the kayak guy
choices.consequence: He looks the most receptive — and the most tired. You choose to use polite-voice on the kayak guy. By Cash Drawer Trouble, the decision has become data, precedent, and a problem larger than the person who made it.

choices.text: Use polite-voice on the pickle lady
choices.consequence: Engaging the indecisive is a customer-service skill. You use polite-voice on the pickle lady. The path to Marcus Found opens, and the system registers the move before anyone admits the rules have changed.

nodes.text: Sandra's drawer is short eleven dollars. Sandra is approximately one held breath away from a kind, sincere meltdown. Garrett, on the floor, is pretending to be busy in the most Garrett way possible. The paths divide here: “Cover the eleven dollars yourself” leads into Corporate, Hiding, while “Help Sandra recount calmly” makes Jonah, Existential the next reckoning.

choices.text: Cover the eleven dollars yourself
choices.consequence: Some kindnesses cost less than they're worth. You choose to cover the eleven dollars yourself. By Corporate, Hiding, the decision has become data, precedent, and a problem larger than the person who made it.

choices.text: Help Sandra recount calmly

nodes.text: Marcus is awake, sort of, behind a wall of bargain DVDs. He swears he was 'organizing.' His apron is on backwards. He says he has 'a great idea about the sprinklers.' This sentence cannot be allowed to develop.

choices.text: Send Marcus to break room jail
choices.consequence: Containment is also management. You choose to send Marcus to break room jail. By Corporate, Hiding, the decision has become data, precedent, and a problem larger than the person who made it.

choices.text: Put Marcus on a small, safe task

nodes.text: Aisle 7. Crouching behind the bulk paper towels with a clipboard. You make eye contact with the corporate inspector. He pretends to be a customer. You both know. “Greet him cheerfully like he isn't a threat” draws you toward The Sprinkler Incident; “Ignore him and run a clean close on principle” leaves Glenn, Crying waiting on the other side.

choices.text: Greet him cheerfully like he isn't a threat

choices.consequence: Don't audition. Just be good. You ignore him and run a clean close on principle. The path to Glenn, Crying opens, and the system registers the move before anyone admits the rules have changed.

nodes.text: Jonah is leaning on the customer service counter mid-monologue — something about late-stage capitalism and shrink rates. Amy is nodding politely while clearly thinking about three other problems. “Cut him off kindly so Amy can breathe” draws you toward The Sprinkler Incident; “Let him finish — he has a point and a clipboard” leaves Glenn, Crying waiting on the other side.

nodes.text: The sprinklers go off in Pets. There is a hamster trying to swim. Dina, somewhere far away, is already running this way at top speed. The paths divide here: “Save the hamster first” leads into Dina Takes Command, while “Cut the sprinklers at the panel” makes Mateo's Schemes the next reckoning.

nodes.text: Glenn is in the break room, gently crying about a viral video of a dog rescuing a duck. He apologizes, twice. He offers you a Werther's. You can hear, faintly, distant sprinklers. To choose “Sit with Glenn for thirty seconds” means meeting Dina Takes Command; “Get him back on the floor — gently” sends you toward Mateo's Schemes instead.

choices.text: Sit with Glenn for thirty seconds

choices.text: Get him back on the floor — gently
choices.consequence: Even Glenn has a closing shift to finish. You choose to get him back on the floor — gently. By Mateo's Schemes, the decision has become data, precedent, and a problem larger than the person who made it.

nodes.text: Dina has appeared with a clipboard, a whistle, and her unstoppable certainty that she should be running things. Half the team obeys her on reflex. The other half disappears into shelving. The distance between Cheyenne's Baby Stroller Emergency and The Customer Who Won't Leave begins with the choice between “Let Dina run the rescue effort” and “Politely take command back.”

nodes.text: Mateo is pitching you — quietly, urgently — on covering up a thing you don't yet know about. 'It's basically not even a problem if no one looks at the security footage,' he whispers. This sentence has been said before. By Mateo.

choices.text: Refuse and tell him to fix it properly
choices.consequence: Friends don't let friends commit retail fraud. You refuse and tell him to fix it properly. The path to Cheyenne's Baby Stroller Emergency opens, and the system registers the move before anyone admits the rules have changed.

choices.text: Listen for one minute, then decide
choices.consequence: Curiosity costs nothing. Yet. You listen for one minute, then decide. The path to The Customer Who Won't Leave opens, and the system registers the move before anyone admits the rules have changed.

nodes.text: Cheyenne's stroller wheel just broke in the parking lot. She's holding the baby and a forty-pack of paper towels and 'fine, I'm fine.' Bo is twenty minutes away. “Send Garrett out to help with the stroller” opens the route to Amy's Quiet Apology. “Go yourself; the floor can wait three minutes” changes the terms and carries you toward Glenn's Speech.

choices.text: Send Garrett out to help with the stroller
choices.consequence: Garrett is secretly the most useful person in this store. You send Garrett out to help with the stroller. The path to Amy's Quiet Apology opens, and the system registers the move before anyone admits the rules have changed.

choices.text: Go yourself; the floor can wait three minutes
choices.consequence: Closing the store starts with closing on your people. You commit to go yourself; the floor can wait three minutes. It carries you toward Glenn's Speech, exchanging a familiar uncertainty for a consequence nobody has modeled.

nodes.text: An older man in Electronics says he's waiting for his nephew. He has been waiting for ninety minutes. He has, you suspect, no nephew. To choose “Sit with him and ask about his day” means meeting Amy's Quiet Apology; “Call him a cab and walk him to the door” sends you toward Glenn's Speech instead.

choices.text: Sit with him and ask about his day
choices.consequence: Loneliness is the slowest checkout line. You sit with him and ask about his day. The path to Amy's Quiet Apology opens, and the system registers the move before anyone admits the rules have changed.

choices.consequence: Kindness can be efficient. You call him a cab and walk him to the door. The path to Glenn's Speech opens, and the system registers the move before anyone admits the rules have changed.

nodes.text: Amy pulls you aside and apologizes for being short with you earlier. She didn't mean it; her morning was hell; she's running on three hours of sleep. You realize, again, why this is your favorite person at this job.

choices.text: Tell her it's fine; sit on the bench a minute
choices.consequence: Friendship is also a closing-shift task. You choose to tell her it's fine; sit on the bench a minute. By The Corporate Verdict, the decision has become data, precedent, and a problem larger than the person who made it.

choices.text: Offer to handle the last items so she can go
choices.consequence: Cover someone tonight; be covered next week. You choose to offer to handle the last items so she can go. By Last Customer Out, the decision has become data, precedent, and a problem larger than the person who made it.

nodes.text: Glenn, recovered, gathers the team near the front and gives a speech that is too long, too sincere, and somehow, by the end, makes you almost cry into your apron about a $9 dollar T-shirt store you all share.

choices.text: Let him finish; nod along
choices.consequence: Earnestness is the secret religion of this place. You let him finish; nod along. The path to The Corporate Verdict opens, and the system registers the move before anyone admits the rules have changed.

choices.text: Wrap him up — there's a corporate man watching
choices.consequence: You commit to wrap him up — there's a corporate man watching. It carries you toward Last Customer Out, exchanging a familiar uncertainty for a consequence nobody has modeled.

nodes.text: The inspector approaches you, expressionless. 'You ran a strange store tonight,' he says. He pauses. 'You ran a good one.' He leaves through the wrong door and sets off an alarm. He pretends he meant to.

choices.text: Bask in the win, quietly
choices.consequence: Compliments at Cloud 9 are like rain — rare and remembered. You commit to bask in the win, quietly. It carries you toward The Parking Lot, exchanging a familiar uncertainty for a consequence nobody has modeled.

choices.text: Pretend you knew it was fine all along
choices.consequence: Confidence is a uniform too. You commit to pretend you knew it was fine all along. It carries you toward Tomorrow, exchanging a familiar uncertainty for a consequence nobody has modeled.

nodes.text: The pickle lady, finally, walks out — with both jars. The kayak guy waves like he just had a really good time. Marcus, miraculously, is in uniform and roughly conscious. “Lock the front doors with ceremony” opens the route to The Parking Lot. “Lock them mid-sentence so nobody comes back” changes the terms and carries you toward Tomorrow.

choices.text: Lock the front doors with ceremony
choices.consequence: Endings deserve a tiny ritual. You choose to lock the front doors with ceremony. By The Parking Lot, the decision has become data, precedent, and a problem larger than the person who made it.

choices.text: Lock them mid-sentence so nobody comes back
choices.consequence: Speed has its own dignity. You lock them mid-sentence so nobody comes back. The path to Tomorrow opens, and the system registers the move before anyone admits the rules have changed.

nodes.text: Eleven of you spill out into the parking lot under the buzzing Cloud 9 sign. Somebody suggests the diner. Somebody else suggests sleeping. Jonah has Opinions about both options. “Go to the diner — these people are your people” opens the route to Booth in the Back. “Go home — you've earned a quiet hour” changes the terms and carries you toward Quiet Hour.

choices.text: Go to the diner — these people are your people
choices.consequence: Workplace family is real family with name tags. You commit to go to the diner — these people are your people. It carries you toward Booth in the Back, exchanging a familiar uncertainty for a consequence nobody has modeled.

choices.consequence: Some nights you cash in solitude. You commit to go home — you've earned a quiet hour. It carries you toward Quiet Hour, exchanging a familiar uncertainty for a consequence nobody has modeled.

nodes.text: You'll do it again tomorrow. The sprinklers, the inspector, the kayak guy, Glenn crying about animals. You don't love every minute. You love most of them, in the strange retail way that you can never quite explain to people who don't work here.

choices.text: Embrace the chaos — this is your life
choices.consequence: There are worse places to be loved. You commit to embrace the chaos — this is your life. It carries you toward The Apron, Hung Up, exchanging a familiar uncertainty for a consequence nobody has modeled.

choices.text: Promise yourself you'll leave by Christmas
choices.consequence: Plans are how you survive the unplanned. You commit to promise yourself you'll leave by Christmas. It carries you toward The Apron, Hung Up, exchanging a familiar uncertainty for a consequence nobody has modeled.

nodes.text: You hang your apron on its hook in the break room and look at the line of identical aprons — your shift, your team, your weird little ecosystem. Whatever you do tomorrow, you did this. The store, against most odds, made it through tonight.

choices.text: Commit to the lifer's pride in the work
choices.consequence: There is dignity in keeping the lights on for someone's dad. You choose to commit to the lifer's pride in the work. By Cloud 9 Lifer, the decision has become data, precedent, and a problem larger than the person who made it.

choices.text: Commit to the leaver's plan, gently
choices.consequence: Saying goodbye well is its own kind of love. You commit to the leaver's plan, gently. The path to By Christmas opens, and the system registers the move before anyone admits the rules have changed.

nodes.text: At the diner you fit eleven people into a booth designed for six. Jonah pays. Mateo doesn't. Amy laughs so hard she snorts, and Glenn says grace and means it. You're tired and shiny-eyed and home — in the strangest possible way.

At home you sit on the floor with the lights off and eat cereal out of the box. Your phone fills with group-chat chaos that you don't open until morning. Tonight you let Cloud 9 be a place you got to leave.

Years later you'll be a regional something or a manager or a customer — and you'll walk past a Cloud 9 and stop for a second, just to listen to the PA and the carts and the laugh of someone you once closed with. It is, somehow, the soundtrack of your twenties.

You make the plan and you almost stick to it. By the time the holiday displays go up you're applying to other things. You'll leave. You'll come back to visit. You'll be the person who tells the new closer 'it's not that bad' and means it.
